text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Nordbanken is managing the share fund which has been the most successful so far this year. The bank's Nordbanken Alfa fund rose 30 percent in six months, boosted by engineering and cyclical shares. The bourse's general index has risen 26 percent in the same period.
- In the past few years union membership has continued to rise, especially among young people and women.

- As of July 1 older workers who have been unemployed for a long time should have been able to collect a new form of compensation from the state. But because of red tape those eligible for the money, estimated at around 7,000 Swedes, will not be able to have the payments for another week.

- Peter Wallenburg was responsible for the ending merger talks between Swedish commercial bank S-E-Banken and state-controlled bank Nordbanken which collapsed earlier this year, according to an interview with Wallenberg in business magazine Manadens Affarer. A couple of analyses show a merger would have been positive for shareholders.

- Swedish property company Castellum has become one of the companies on the Stockholm Stock Exchange's with the highest concentration of foreign ownership. Some 40 percent of its shares are held by foreigners. Only Tornet has a higher percentage of overseas owners.
- Tax on petrol in Sweden rises 0.25 crown from July 1. Sweden has some of the highest petrol prices in Europe.

- A share fund at Stockholm brokerage Erik Penser which is run by a computer has outperformed all others in Sweden, rising over 31 percent in the first half of the year. Funds with shares from small companies have performed worst.

- Foreign investors are once again investing in Swedish shares. Statistics show they sold shares for 13 billion crowns for five months running and they bought shares for 500 million crowns net in May. Foreign investors have also returned to Swedish government bonds. Soon foreign holding of the papers will return to 1994 levels.

- Half of all new businesses are set up in Sweden's biggest cities, with Stockholm topping the list. Last year some 58,795 companies were created, according to data from a group called Jobs and Society.
